claim: A 4th-century Chinese first-aid handbook told readers to soak a handful of qinghao (sweet wormwood) in water and drink the juice for fevers. In the 1970s Tu Youyou read that line and it led her team to artemisinin, now a frontline malaria drug.
evidence: A handful of qinghao immersed with 2 liters of water, wring out the juice and drink it all
source: Tu Y. The discovery of artemisinin (qinghaosu) and gifts from Chinese medicine. Nature Medicine 17(10): 1217-1220, 2011
locator: quoting Ge Hong, Zhouhou Beiji Fang (Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies)
author: Tu Youyou
licence: Copyright; quote one short credited line only
caveat: Tu won the 2015 Nobel Prize for this. Modern artemisinin drugs are purified and dosed; drinking wormwood juice is NOT a malaria treatment. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Deep dive candidate: 1,600 years from a handbook to a Nobel

claim: A 2024 BMJ review of randomised trials found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all reduced depression, with walking/jogging among the strongest.
evidence: walking or jogging (n=1210, κ=51, Hedges’ g −0.62, 95% credible interval −0.80 to −0.45)
source: Noetel M et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ 384: e075847, 2024
author: Noetel et al.
caveat: Not a replacement for treatment; say 'alongside', never 'instead of'. Many trials were low certainty.
use_in: Reel: 'A walk is in the depression guidelines now'

claim: Marcus: when you've done someone a good turn, why look for a third thing, like credit or a favour back?
evidence: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these
author: Marcus Aurelius

claim: Knowing others is clever; knowing yourself is wiser.
evidence: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
author: Laozi (attributed)
